A confirmed case of meningitis is defined as the isolation or identification of the causal pathogen (e.g., Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae type b) from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of a suspected or probable case through culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or agglutination tests. Operational thresholds are criteria that trigger specific actions to prepare for an epidemic (alert threshold) or respond to an epidemic (epidemic threshold) in health districts, sub-districts, or populations at risk. The alert threshold is a level of incidence that prompts actions such as strengthening surveillance, confirming cases, distributing treatment protocols, and informing authorities. The epidemic threshold is a higher level of incidence that triggers epidemic responses, including mass vaccination, antibiotic distribution, and raising public awareness. The meningitis belt of sub-Saharan Africa spans the continent from Senegal to Ethiopia. This region is prone to major epidemics of meningococcal meningitis, which have high case fatality rates and serious sequelae, placing a heavy burden on national and local health services. Historically, most epidemics were caused by Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A (NmA), and WHO guidelines have primarily focused on controlling these outbreaks. However, since 2010, countries in the meningitis belt have introduced a new serogroup A meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenAfriVac), which is expected to provide long-lasting individual protection and herd immunity. Other serogroups, such as NmW, NmX, and NmC, continue to cause epidemics, albeit less frequently and on a smaller scale. Due to these changes in the epidemiological pattern of meningitis, WHO established a Guideline Development Group to review evidence and recommendations for epidemic control in the meningitis belt. Four main topics were selected for review: operational thresholds for outbreak investigation and response, rapid diagnostic tests in outbreak management, antibiotic regimens during epidemics, and prophylaxis for household contacts of cases. This guideline does not include recommendations on vaccines already covered in existing WHO guidance. The evidence was collected through systematic searches for surveillance data (for questions on operational thresholds and antibiotic regimens) or systematic literature reviews (for questions on rapid diagnostic tests and household prophylaxis). The quality of the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework and was rated as low or very low for most questions. To move from evidence to recommendations, the DECIDE framework was used to evaluate the priority of the problem, quality of evidence, benefits and harms, values and preferences, resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility before reaching a recommendation. Of the 16 recommendations developed, four were strong recommendations made in favor of an intervention where potential benefits clearly outweighed any potential harms. The remaining 12 recommendations were conditional. For operational thresholds, it is recommended that vaccination campaigns be implemented as soon as possible and within four weeks of crossing the epidemic threshold (strong recommendation; low-quality evidence). For populations of 30,000–100,000, the recommended alert threshold is three cases per 100,000 people in a week (strong recommendation; low-quality evidence). For populations under 30,000, the alert threshold is either two cases in one week or a higher incidence than in a non-epidemic year (conditional recommendation; expert opinion). The epidemic threshold for populations of 30,000–100,000 is 10 cases per 100,000 people in a week (conditional recommendation; low-quality evidence). For populations under 30,000, the epidemic threshold is five cases in one week or a doubling of incidence in a three-week period (conditional recommendation; expert opinion). Vaccination is recommended for populations adjacent to epidemic areas if they are considered at risk (conditional recommendation; expert opinion). In special situations, such as mass gatherings, refugee camps, or closed institutions like schools or barracks, an immediate response, including mass vaccination, is recommended when two cases of meningococcal disease are confirmed in one week (conditional recommendation; expert opinion). Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), such as latex agglutination or immunochromatography dipsticks, are recommended for use in investigating meningitis outbreaks (conditional recommendation; low-quality evidence). If RDTs are positive for a vaccine-preventable serogroup, verification of the serogroup by PCR or culture is recommended before initiating a vaccine response (strong recommendation; expert opinion). For antibiotic regimens during epidemics, a seven-day course of ceftriaxone is recommended for treating suspected bacterial meningitis in children under two months of age (conditional recommendation; expert opinion). For adults and children aged two months and older, a five-day course of ceftriaxone is recommended (conditional recommendation; very low-quality evidence). For prophylaxis of household contacts, antibiotics are recommended as a prophylactic measure for all ages during non-epidemic periods but not during epidemics (conditional recommendation; very low-quality evidence). Ciprofloxacin is the preferred prophylactic agent, with ceftriaxone as an alternative when ciprofloxacin is contraindicated (conditional recommendation; very low-quality evidence). Rifampicin is not recommended for use as a prophylactic agent (strong recommendation; low-quality evidence). Vaccination is not recommended for household contacts (conditional recommendation; low-quality evidence). For over 100 years, major epidemics of meningococcal disease have occurred periodically within the African meningitis belt, which spans from Senegal to Ethiopia. These epidemics are highly disruptive, requiring the establishment of emergency treatment centers and placing a severe strain on routine health services. Most epidemics have been caused by Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A (NmA), with some due to serogroups W, X, and C. However, outbreaks due to serogroups B and Y have been conspicuously absent. Hypervirulent clonal complexes ST-5 (mainly serogroup A) and ST-11 (mainly serogroup W) have accounted for most epidemics in this region. Following the introduction of MenAfriVac, NmW has become the predominant serogroup. Consequently, the threshold incidence rates and population bases for interventions may no longer be valid, and the recommendations for managing epidemic meningitis in the meningitis belt need to be reviewed. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) support urgent decision-making for outbreak management. RDTs can discriminate between various bacterial species causing meningitis and, for Neisseria meningitidis, between serogroups A, C, W, and Y, but not X. Identifying the predominant bacterial agent and meningococcal serogroup in outbreaks has become increasingly important.
